name: Adam Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, without ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what happens on your factory shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am junior on a bottle labelling line, watching each label land straight and checking the guide rail when bottles drift. I finished secondary school and have only been here a short time, so I call the senior operator before touching a setting I do not know. The factory pays me less than experienced operators.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is happening at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Samira works part time at a pharmacy, and our two school-age children and mortgage leave us about three weeks of savings. There are few similar factory jobs nearby. I use AI now and then to understand a phrase in the manual, but I want a proven fix shown on the actual machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the label-line crew that AI can write a nicer maintenance note, but somebody still has to catch a crooked label. I would say that over tea, not make a speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am still on the junior rate and the mortgage takes most of it. My wife Samira works part time at a pharmacy, and our two school-age children need lunches and bus fares; three weeks of savings makes even an ordinary plant stoppage hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep watching the bottle labeller and ask the senior operator to show me a faster way to align the guide rail. I would add a small new amount from each full week’s wage to our emergency pot only after the mortgage and food clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though the AI itself is quiet. A week without pay would be louder than any computer story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the label go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wet bottle slides a fraction as the roller catches it, leaving the label high on one shoulder. I stop the belt and check the rail with the senior operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then I ask a chatbot to explain a phrase in the machine manual. It helps with words, but I still need the senior operator beside me for the real adjustment.

say: I would tell the **label crew** that a neat note cannot fix a crooked bottle label.
I would ask the **senior operator** for a practical guide-rail check.
think: My **junior pay** and mortgage leave little spare money.
Samira’s **part-time wage** and three weeks saved do not cover a long stoppage.
do: Keep watching the **bottle labeller** and learn the rail alignment from a colleague.
Add **fresh wages** to the emergency pot only after mortgage and food are paid.
feel: **Anxious** about an ordinary missed week, even with little AI change.
S0.quote: A week without pay would be louder than any computer story.
fieldNote: Adam uses AI **occasionally** for manual wording, without claiming this is a new technical skill.
His **baseline mortgage pressure** and very thin savings keep the plateau from feeling secure.

steps.text: Keep checking bottle labels and guide-rail alignment
Save fresh wages after the mortgage and food clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the canteen that faster orders are fine if the delivery schedule is honest. I would want the plant to tell us before it changes the packing rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An AI schedule may cut the office’s paperwork first, but cameras and stacking arms could make junior label shifts shorter later. My wife’s part-time pharmacy work would not cover the mortgage if I lost two days a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the line job and compare the next four paid rosters with the old hours. If the plant offers a paid demonstration of a new label-check camera, I would watch and ask what it misses; after two shorter rosters I would apply only for posted nearby machine jobs that cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I have learned to try a proven thing, but I cannot call a shorter payslip an experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could the camera miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bottle can turn after the camera and peel the label at the final roller. I would show the supervisor a failed bottle before accepting the new count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you operate the camera after watching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the plant offers paid hands-on practice and the guard is checked. Watching a demonstration is not learning a new control.

say: I would ask for **rota notice** before office scheduling changes the label line.
I would watch a **paid camera demonstration** and show missed defects.
think: My **junior shifts** could shrink when cameras and arms spread.
Samira’s **part-time pay** would not cover the mortgage after a large cut.
do: Compare **four paid rosters** before deciding whether hours have changed.
Watch the **camera demonstration** if offered on paid time.
Apply after **two short rosters** to posted nearby bill-covering machine jobs.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic cut to the family’s wage.
S1.quote: I cannot call a shorter payslip an experiment.
fieldNote: He asks to **watch a demonstration**, with hands-on learning separately conditional on offered paid guarded practice.
The job application needs **two shorter rosters** and an actual nearby posting with household-covering pay.

steps.text: Keep label-line job and compare four paid rosters
Watch a paid label-camera demonstration if offered
Apply after two short rosters to posted nearby bill-covering machine job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI may plan bottle runs by 2028 when I am forty five, but robots that handle the line arrive around 2031 when I am forty eight. Three years is not much with a mortgage and two children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the simpler labelling and stacking hours to go once the robots work. I am junior, the savings cover only weeks, and Samira’s part-time wage would not replace mine; I would lie awake over the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cut takeaway meals and the planned car repair that can wait, then ask for the written staffing plan. If my hours fall, I would apply for a posted local line job at bill-covering pay with paid safe instruction, and I would ask family about temporary help if no such job is available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by a likely major pay loss. I can make a list of calls, but it will not pay next month’s mortgage on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which car repair can wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The seat upholstery can wait; the brakes cannot. I would cut the unnecessary work and keep the car safe for the school and factory trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take unpaid training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would need an offered paid place and a posted job at enough pay before enrolling in a course. We have too little cash to buy a promise.

say: I would say **2028 planning AI** arrives before capable line robots around 2031.
I would ask for a **written staffing plan** before junior hours are removed.
think: I expect **labelling hours** to fall when robots handle the line.
Our **few weeks saved** and part-time pharmacy income cannot cover a long mortgage gap.
do: Cut **takeaway and upholstery** while keeping essential car safety work.
Apply after **lost hours** for a posted bill-covering local job with paid safe instruction.
Ask **family for temporary help** if no adequate job appears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless mortgage worry.
S2.quote: I can make a list of calls, but it will not pay next month’s mortgage on its own.
fieldNote: Adam expects a **major junior-hour loss** and explicitly lies awake over housing costs.
His fallback application needs a **real posting**, bill-covering pay and safe paid instruction; family help follows a failed search.

steps.text: Cut takeaway meals and nonessential car upholstery
Apply after lost hours for posted bill-covering local line job with paid safe instruction
Ask family for temporary help if no adequate local job appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the planning system comes in 2031 when I am forty eight, and capable hands-on robots around 2034 when I am fifty one. Five years might let me learn a different machine while the labeller still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot promise the mortgage will be small enough by then. But if the plant still has work, I could qualify for maintenance on a real line, rather than wait for the junior shift to disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the labeller shift and ask about a fully funded electrical maintenance course with paid workshop days. If the plant offers a place and a posted nearby maintenance role pays our bills, I would enrol; after qualification I would apply for that job only if the safe isolation duties are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan worth checking. I learn better after someone proves the repair on a stopped machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified fitter would isolate the labeller and show me how to test a failed sensor before replacing it. A manual alone would not make me safe testing a bottle-labeller sensor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only an unpaid evening course exists?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paid shift and ask again when a funded place opens. Samira and I cannot lose work hours to study without a real job at the end.

say: I would distinguish **2031 office change** from 2034 robots on the label line.
I would ask for **practical maintenance training** on a stopped machine.
think: The **mortgage** still needs my junior wage during the warning.
A **maintenance qualification** only helps with a real adequate local job.
do: Keep the **paid labeller shift** while checking training options.
Enrol in **funded paid-time electrical training** only with an offered place and posted bill-covering role.
Apply after **qualification** only with written safe isolation duties.
feel: **Anxious**, with a course and job route to verify.
S3.quote: A manual alone would not make me safe testing a bottle-labeller sensor.
fieldNote: Adam accepts proven practical learning, but **paid time and funding** must protect household income.
The later **job application** requires qualification, a posted adequate local role and written isolation duties.

steps.text: Keep paid labeller shift while training options are checked
Enrol in funded paid electrical course if offered place and posted bill-covering job exist
Apply after qualifying to posted nearby bill-covering maintenance job with written safe isolation duties

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am fifty three, with capable bottle-line robots around 2039 when I am fifty six. Thirteen years before a physical robot gives time, but the mortgage starts again every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be older then, but I cannot assume either child will pay our bills. I may still need full wages at fifty six, and less than a month saved today means I have to use the years well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, in 2026, I would keep the label shift and add a new small amount from full wages to the emergency pot after bills. In the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would check actual rosters and local postings; if paid hours have fallen for two months I would apply only for a posted bill-covering role with safe paid instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the mortgage now, though I can use a longer warning. I would rather see a real offer than tell the children a robot date will take care of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you wait until 2036 to learn anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If the plant offers funded paid practical training with a posted adequate job sooner, I would consider it once the method has been proven on a stopped line. I would not pay for an unoffered course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What monthly amount can you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only whatever a full week leaves after the mortgage, food and school fares. I will write down the transfer rather than announce a number that might fail.

say: I would say **2036 thinking AI** precedes 2039 bottle-line robots.
I would ask for **real offers** instead of treating a robot date as a plan.
think: At **fifty six**, I may still need a full wage for household bills.
Thin **current savings** mean the longer warning cannot be wasted.
do: Keep the **label shift** and save new wages after essential bills.
Check **post-2036 rosters** and apply after two reduced months only to posted adequate safe work.
feel: **Anxious** about current mortgage pressure, with time to prepare.
S4.quote: I would rather see a real offer than tell the children a robot date will take care of us.
fieldNote: Adam distinguishes **2026 paid work** from conditional work and applications after 2036.
His extra saving is **new wages after bills**, and the later job move needs two cut months and an adequate safe posting.

steps.text: Keep current labeller shift while paid and safe
Save fresh pay only after mortgage, food and school fares
Apply after two reduced months to posted bill-covering safe local role

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could remove junior label shifts by 2031 while our mortgage still needs two wages. An honest staffing plan, paid practical training and posted local bill-covering jobs would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how many full wage packets a family needs before a new certificate pays anything. A label machine can stop for an hour, but the mortgage keeps running.

headlineQuote: A label machine can stop for an hour, but the mortgage keeps running.
portrait: **Adam**, 43, is a junior bottle-line operator with secondary schooling and limited time on the machine.
His **low pay**, part-time household second wage, two children, mortgage, three weeks saved and few local jobs make lost hours serious.
He uses AI **occasionally** for wording, but adopts machinery only after safe practical proof and paid instruction.
The fast case brings **expected wage loss**; longer warnings help only if funded training leads to a real adequate job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove Adam’s junior label shifts around 2031 before his household builds a reserve.
whatWouldHelp: A written **staffing plan**, paid practical training and posted bill-covering local jobs would help.
